Letter to the Governor
Dear Governor Inslee,
We are glad to hear that your administration is seeking out a diverse range of
opinions in an eﬀort to inform policy making in your state around self-driving
and cooperative vehicles. As America moves further into the 21st century, the
pervasiveness and rapid advancement of technology in nearly every aspect of
daily life can sometimes feel daunting. For example, in the case of driverless

spans.text: cars, it is not a trivial matter to assess potential risks and rewards for individual

lines.text: cars, it is not a trivial matter to assess potential risks and rewards for individual
drivers and for society as a whole.
While we are far from providing a comprehensive study of this issue in our
model for the eﬀect of driverless vehicles on traﬃc patterns, we feel that a few
of our central results can provide some insight for lawmakers seeking to craft

spans.text: laws and regulations, make decisions about investment in certain infrastructures,

lines.text: laws and regulations, make decisions about investment in certain infrastructures,
and communicate eﬀectively with constituents about the eﬀects of self-driving
cars on our roads.
The ﬁrst of these is that although increasing the amount of self-driving cars
as a percentage of vehicles on highways is projected to relieve the burden of
heavy traﬃc to some extent, these beneﬁts would quite likely be outweighed if
the total number of vehicles were to increase. In other words, even if relaxing
the driving age for these vehicles or providing tax incentives to use them may

spans.text: seem promising politically, these are actions which might encourage more people

lines.text: seem promising politically, these are actions which might encourage more people
to drive, which has the potential to worsen overall traﬃc conditions.
That being said, our models indicate that self-driving and/or cooperative cars
far outperform conventional drivers when it comes to changing lanes and merg-

spans.text: As the city of Seattle (and the broader King County area) reckon with the chal-

lines.text: As the city of Seattle (and the broader King County area) reckon with the chal-
lenges of adapting infrastructure designed and built in the late 20th century to
current 21st century demands, technological advances such as self-driving, co-
operative vehicles may oﬀer some respite. However, before investing signiﬁcant
time and resources in accommodating such vehicles, it is desirable to know to

spans.text: what extent they are capable of mitigating the traﬃc jams that occur with some

lines.text: what extent they are capable of mitigating the traﬃc jams that occur with some
regularity on busy commuter highways. Here, we investigate the eﬀect of the
ratio of self-driving and/or cooperative vehicles to conventional vehicles on the
road, with the goal of identifying points of either diminishing or particularly
increased returns with respect to improving traﬃc ﬂow. This is accomplished
by developing a model for traﬃc ﬂow as a function of volume demand and road
capacity, and subsequently applying the model to real-world data.

listed references and those in parentheses refer to the numbered equations.
Assumptions and Justiﬁcations
In the literature of traﬃc ﬂow modeling, there are three general paradigms:
microscopic, mesoscopic, and macroscopic [1, 2, 3, 4]. These paradigms treat
traﬃc as discreet vehicles, modular groups of vehicles, or a continuous ﬂow of

spans.text: In the ﬁrst part of our model, designed to describe broader

lines.text: vehicles, respectively. In the ﬁrst part of our model, designed to describe broader
trends and patterns in traﬃc ﬂow, we chose to analyze the problem from the
macroscopic view, for the following reasons. First, the data provided are not
granular enough to be easily applied to microscopic formulae (i.e. behavior of
individual cars/drivers); second, the structure of equations in the macroscopic

spans.text: model are more amenable to numerical analysis such as ﬁnite diﬀerence methods;

lines.text: model are more amenable to numerical analysis such as ﬁnite diﬀerence methods;
third, the macroscopic paradigm is well-established in the ﬁeld of traﬃc ﬂow
modeling and we therefore reason that it has at least a baseline capability to
describe emergent patterns [1, 2, 3]. This is the main assumption shaping the
basic structure of our ﬁrst model.
The second part of our model, designed to describe lane changing behavior,
we consider the interaction of individual vehicles on the microscopic level. In
this context the microscopic approach makes more sense, because a change in
lane is a discreet event.
Additional assumptions are listed below, and while we provide justiﬁcation
for all of them, they could generally be adjusted to reﬂect more realistic condi-
tions, given additional time and computing resources.

Lane Change Model
Another main aspect in traﬃc ﬂow is the interactions among vehicles as they
change their lanes. A change of lane occurs when ramp vehicles merge into
a highway stream, highway vehicles leave for minor roads, and when vehicles
change into a diﬀerent lane of the route to prepare to turn or leave the road.

rejected gaps longer than it. Thus, an average vehicle would decide to merge
if a gap is larger than the critical gap.

Weaknesses of the ﬂow-density-mean speed model include the follow-
ing:
• The model does not account for interchanges or merging lanes in traﬃc
and their eﬀects on the mean speed or traﬃc density.
• The model does not account for cooperation between self-driving cars or
the interaction between self-driving and non-self-driving cars.
• The model does not account for diﬀerences in car length of self-driving
cars from the current average car length.
• The results presented made use of an invariant, daily, peak traﬃc hours
distribution which was bimodal in nature which does not account for the
diﬀerence in typical traﬃc and holiday or weekend traﬃc.
